I love that we not only had to figure out the theme answers, but the clues as well!

All the theme answers – every single one – were clever and marvelous.  The clue for NEEDS NO INTRODUCTION – [_raves] – had me knitting my brow for quite a while, and brought a big aha when its solution finally hit me.

There were also quite a few slippery clues for the non-theme answers – for example, [Untold] for A TON OF and [Closely following] for TRUE TO.

So, plenty of puzzling and plenty of entertainment – a sterling Sunday.  Bravo, Sam.  This hit my happy button.  Thank you!

I just have seen this theme or a version of it So. Darn. Often. and there was just nothing fresh or exciting about it, in my opinion. Personally, I would rather see a hundred Mario puzzles, goofy puns, or other big passionate swings that may be  a miss for some but still make me sit up and take notice.

It was fun to also guess what the missing letter(s) would be.  Sometimes there was only one possibility, like with the DOCTORS and the knight and the dialog -- but would it be SAGA or SAGE?  FRANK or FRANC?  CRAVES, GRAVES or BRAVES?

I enjoyed the puzzle and it's theme, but CRAVES isn't a synonym for NEEDS. Crave means "intense desire," which is wanting something, not needing it. I may be craving a piece of dark chocolate right now, but that doesn't mean I need it. And while I know a clue is not the same as a definition, this clue/answer pair was the weak point in this puzzle. The rest were clever and fun and apt.

How is "exgi" even a word? More importantly how does “vet” (what I understand is to cull or selectively extract) a relevant clue? From Google/AI:

Exegi is the first-person singular perfect active indicative form of the Latin verb exigō, meaning "I have exacted," "I have finished," or "I have driven out".

I fully understand the concept of “poetic license” – poetry has a flow that makes such integrated "errors" pleasing to recognize.

However, I now know there’s also a “puzzle constructor’s license”.  Regardless, when a back-breaker like today’s puzzle contains an alternate? spelling of a somewhat obscure Latin term, it really takes the wind out of one’s sails.

@Nicholas Mitchell Thanks. Yeah, I got that part but I thought the missing letters, when put together, would form a phrase or sentence or something. ... Do you mean 36 Across? I don't get "CRAVES" either. Haven't checked all the comments for an explanation.

@B

If there's a beef to be had here, it's that "craves" doesn't really line up with "needs," but then again, neither does "wants."  "Requires" works better in my opinion, and there's no need to "misdirect" by using a poorly lined up semi-equivalent when there's a more accurate one out there.

But I'm not sure how you can impute laziness here.  Finding examples for the clue is not hard.  The constructor didn't get lazy because he wrote a clue that could have been better.  The key for the solver is mainly to get the actual answers, and secondarily to figure out what letter is missing in the clue.

It would have also been more elegant if the missing letters spelled something related, but that would be asking for what is probably impossible.
